source: Ko and Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies in unfamiliar programming systems
finding: Baseline for this subfield. 75 people debugged a Stata program with four planted bugs in 20 minutes. Clustering of logged actions gave three comprehension strategies. Success tracked bug-specific domain knowledge and attitude more than strategy.
numbers: 86 recruited, 75 analysed. Clusters: n=20 (depth-first, info-seeking), n=40 (inactive, inspects spec/graph), n=15 (breadth-first, most experienced). Mean bugs fixed (0-4): 1.00 (SD .97), 1.65 (.98), 2.00 (1.07).
quote: bug-specific domain knowledge was the best predictor of debugging success
limits: Exploratory. Authors say 75 is small for hierarchical clustering and that comparing clusters on the measures that define them is risky. Single task, Stata, students.
agent_relevance: Human anchor for angle C: the question for models is whether a strategy label changes outcome once relevant knowledge is held fixed.

source: Ko and Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies in unfamiliar programming systems (cluster test)
finding: Correction to the common summary 'no strategy was best'. The paper itself found clusters 2 and 3 fixed more bugs than cluster 1 (p<.05), but said strategies 2 and 3 were comparable and no strategy was particularly successful (few fixed more than 3 bugs).
numbers: Main effect on average bugs fixed, post-hoc cluster 2 and 3 > cluster 1, p<.05. Cluster linked to programming experience p<.01 and attitude to the experiment p<.01 (cluster 3 most positive).
limits: Cluster 1 may have lost out by sinking time into one command (valueofoutlier), so depth-first was not clearly bad in general.
agent_relevance: The schema should not claim strategy is irrelevant. Strategy is second to knowledge, and a strategy that fixes attention on one hard thing costs coverage.

source: Ko and Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies in unfamiliar programming systems (bug-level)
finding: Success on the inverted-axes bug (needs reading the output graph) went with statistics-software experience, self-reported math and computer experience, and time spent looking at the graph output. Statistics test mean was .40 for fixers versus .31 for non-fixers on that bug.
numbers: Inverted axes bug fixed by about 21 percent of 75 (Table 5 total row; layout garbled in text extraction). Other three bugs showed no statistics-test difference (.31-.34 vs .31-.32).
limits: Correlational. Table 3 results are per bug and not adjusted for multiple tests.
agent_relevance: Task-relevant knowledge decides which hypothesis the agent can even form. Retrieve domain facts before choosing strategy.

source: Ko and Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies in unfamiliar programming systems (contradicting comment)
finding: A misleading code comment made one bug (valueofoutlier range) much easier to find. Nearly twice as many found it as found the matching bug in the pvalue command. Finding one helped find the sibling.
numbers: Authors: nearly twice as many participants found valueofoutlier range as pvalue range; fixers of one were more likely to fix the other.
limits: Observational reading of Table 2, no test reported.
agent_relevance: Cues in the artefact (comments, spec-code mismatches) can substitute for strategy. Treat contradictions as a first-class signal.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Self-repair (model debugs its own code) gives small, inconsistent gains once total sample budget is counted. The bottleneck is the quality of the diagnosis feedback, not the repair step. LLM version of knowledge beating strategy.
numbers: Models: Code Llama, GPT-3.5, GPT-4; HumanEval and APPS (300 random APPS tasks). GPT-4 on APPS beats no-repair baseline by up to 8 percent; GPT-3.5 marginal gains only at largest np; up to 34 percent relative gain for GPT-3.5 on competition problems.
quote: using a stronger model to provide feedback produces substantially larger gains
limits: Gains depend on how sample budget is accounted. Not about human strategies.
agent_relevance: Do not spend budget on repair loops by default. Spend it on better diagnosis (stronger or independent critic).

source: Olausson et al. (2023) feedback source test
finding: Swapping a weak model's own feedback for a stronger model's feedback let weaker models beat both baseline and their own self-repair on APPS. On HumanEval Code Llama gained more as the feedback model got stronger (GPT-3.5 then GPT-4).
numbers: Pairs: Code Llama+GPT-3.5, Code Llama+GPT-4 (HumanEval); Code Llama+GPT-3.5, GPT-3.5+GPT-4 (APPS). np in 1..25, nf=nr=1.
limits: Uses a stronger model, so cost is higher and not a pure same-model test.
agent_relevance: Knowledge of what is wrong (the critic) matters more than loop shape. Matches the Ko and Uttl bug-knowledge result.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) human feedback experiment
finding: Expert human diagnosis fed to GPT-4 raised repair success from 33.30 to 52.60 percent overall (1.58x). The gap widened with task difficulty.
numbers: 16 participants, 2 feedbacks each for 40 failing GPT-4 programs, 25 repairs per feedback. GPT-4 feedback vs human: introductory 42.64 vs 62.21; interview 19.33 vs 45.67; competition 3.67 vs 14.67.
limits: Small sample, one hour per participant. Authors say it is not a human-in-the-loop comparison.
agent_relevance: Same repair strategy gives very different outcomes depending on the diagnostic knowledge supplied.

source: Huang et al. (2023) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Without an oracle label, asking a model to review and fix its own answer does not help and often hurts. With oracle labels the same loop looks strong, which inflated earlier claims.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7 over rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0. With oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3 (as read from table), GPT-4 95.5 -> 97.5.
quote: these results can only be regarded as indicative of an oracle's performance
limits: Reasoning tasks, not debugging. Table text extraction is jumbled; values read in row order.
agent_relevance: Any self-check operator needs an external signal (tests, tool output). Otherwise it is a strategy with no knowledge behind it.

source: Huang et al. (2023) answer-change analysis
finding: Most harm comes from changing correct answers. On GSM8K GPT-3.5 kept 74.7 percent of answers unchanged; on CommonSenseQA it changed more because wrong options looked plausible.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5: 74.7% no change (from Figure 2 text).
limits: Percentages parsed from text near the figure; approximate.
agent_relevance: Guard: do not revise an answer unless new evidence arrives.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
finding: Same model, same task, different interface gives large swings. A plain shell agent solved far fewer SWE-bench Lite tasks than GPT-4 Turbo with tailored commands. Interface design acted as encoded knowledge.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: shell-only GPT-4 Turbo 7.33%; SWE-agent GPT-4 Turbo 18.00% (full split 12.47%). Ablation on 300 tasks: no custom edit command 10.3 vs 18.0; no search 15.7; iterative search 12.0; summarized search 18.0.
limits: Ablations on GPT-4 only. Small-subset results have wide standard errors.
agent_relevance: Tool surface and feedback format can matter as much as thinking strategy. Treat the interface as part of the schema.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent behaviour analysis
finding: Trajectories nearly always start by writing a reproduction script or by localizing (find_file/search_dir). One-by-one iterative search made agents inspect every hit and did worse than no search tool at all.
numbers: Iterative search 12.0 vs no search 15.7 on the 300-task subset. Most common action triple: create, edit, python (reproduce).
limits: Behavioural description from one agent design.
agent_relevance: Matches the human finding that depth-first fixation on one item costs coverage (Ko and Uttl cluster 1). Cap per-hypothesis effort.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: A fixed three-phase pipeline (localize, repair, validate) with no agent choice of next action matched or beat open-ended agent strategies at low cost. Strategy freedom was not the source of performance.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: Agentless 32.00% (96/300) at $0.70; SWE-agent Claude 3.5 Sonnet 23.00%; SWE-agent GPT-4o 18.33% at $1.62; AutoCodeRover 19.00-21.67%.
limits: Leaderboard includes closed systems with different LLMs. Cost and rank as of the paper (2024).
agent_relevance: Supports a scaffold with a fixed skeleton and strict phases over free strategy.

source: Xia et al. (2024) benchmark audit
finding: Manual audit of SWE-bench Lite found issues that leak the answer or mislead, so some success comes from knowledge handed in the issue text, not strategy.
numbers: Exact ground-truth patch in the issue text: 4.3% of Lite problems (text); misleading solution in description: 5.0%. Only 94 reproduction tests printed 'Issue resolved' on the ground-truth patch.
limits: The paper's chart also shows 3.0% for exact patch; cite 4.3 with care.
agent_relevance: Evaluate on cleaned subsets, or knowledge leakage will look like strategy skill.

source: Meng et al. (2024) LLM-based Agents for Automated Bug Fixing: How Far Are We?
finding: Six top SWE-bench Verified systems with different designs mostly solve the same issues. Solvability depends more on the issue than on the system.
numbers: 500 cases: 404 solved by at least one of six tools, 96 by none, 181 by all six. Best tool resolved 64.6%.
limits: Leaderboard systems, designs partly private.
agent_relevance: Shared failure on the same cases suggests missing information, not a wrong strategy choice.

source: Meng et al. (2024) localization versus repair
finding: File-level localization accuracy tracks resolution rank. One system with poor localization still repaired at a high rate once it localized correctly.
numbers: W&B Programmer hit at least one buggy file in 448 cases (all buggy files in 394); Learn-by-interact 342, a 31.0% gap. Given a correct file, Learn-by-interact resolved 281/342 = 82.2%; W&B 69.6%.
limits: Conditional rates mix different case sets; not causal.
agent_relevance: Localizing the fault (knowing where) is the high-leverage step. Put effort budget there.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench: Evaluating Debugging Capability of LLMs
finding: Debug success depends strongly on bug type. Syntax and reference bugs are easy, logic and multi-bug cases are hard, for humans and models. Skill looks like bug-class knowledge, not one strategy.
numbers: 4,253 instances, 4 major and 18 minor bug types, C++, Java, Python. GPT-4 passes 75.0%, GPT-3.5 62.1%, both below human. Model fixes a bug in under 10 s versus about 20 minutes for humans.
limits: Bugs implanted by GPT-4 into LeetCode code, so synthetic.
agent_relevance: Mirrors Ko and Uttl: per-bug-type knowledge predicts success. Route by suspected bug class.

source: Tian et al. (2024) runtime feedback effect
finding: Runtime traceback helps syntax and reference bugs but does not help, and can disrupt, logic bugs. A uniform run-and-read strategy is not uniformly good.
numbers: Shown in Figure 4 for gpt-4-0613 and gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 (numeric values not read from the figure).
limits: Qualitative only here.
agent_relevance: Condition operators on bug type. Do not always feed raw traces back for logic errors.

source: Tian et al. (2024) debugging versus coding
finding: For closed models, fixing syntax or reference errors is easier than writing the code, but logic and multi-error fixing is as hard or harder. Coding and debugging skill correlate.
numbers: Same LeetCode problems, GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 (Figure 5).
limits: Two models only.
agent_relevance: Debug ability is not a separate strategy skill apart from knowledge of the problem.

source: Kang et al. (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: A scaffold that forces hypothesis, prediction, experiment with a real debugger, observation, conclusion roughly matches but does not beat plain LLM repair. It adds explanations and a confidence signal.
numbers: Defects4J v1.2 correct fixes: AutoSD 76 vs LLM-Base 87 (Recoder 24, InCoder 41); v2.0: 113 vs 110 (Recoder 11, InCoder 28). ARHE benchmark: similar to LLM-Base.
limits: Codex-era models, 2023. Competitive, not superior.
agent_relevance: The scientific-method strategy (human-derived) did not raise accuracy. Its value was verifiability.

source: Kang et al. (2023) <DONE> confidence and debugger ablation
finding: A model-emitted <DONE> after real debugger experiments signals higher precision. When debugger output was hallucinated by the LLM, the signal reversed.
numbers: With plausible patch: 89% correct when <DONE> predicted vs 82% without. With LLM-simulated debugger results, <DONE> solutions were 11 percentage points less likely to be plausible.
limits: Defects4J sample of 100 patches with and without <DONE>; modest difference.
agent_relevance: Confidence is informative only when grounded in real execution. Never simulate tool output.

source: Kang et al. (2023) human study
finding: 20 participants (8 undergraduate, 6 graduate, 6 professionals with 3-10 years) judged patch correctness with and without AutoSD explanations. Accuracy was higher with explanations in 5 of 6 real-world bugs, time about equal.
numbers: 20 participants, 12 bugs, explanations shown in a random 3 of 6 cases per person. Explanations rated helpful in two thirds of bugs; 70% agreed explanations are important.
limits: Small N. Professionals more mixed than students.
agent_relevance: Explanations help human reviewers more than they raise machine accuracy.

source: Jimenez et al. (2023) SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
finding: Giving the right files (oracle context) more than doubles the resolve rate of the best model versus sparse retrieval. Knowing where to look dominates.
numbers: Claude 2 resolves 1.96% with BM25 retrieval and 4.8% with oracle retrieval. BM25 retrieves a superset of oracle files in about 40% of instances at the 27k-token limit.
limits: 2023 models; later agents are far higher.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM parallel to bug-specific knowledge: same model improves when relevant context is present.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: Rubber-duck style debugging (model explains its own code, optionally with execution trace) improves accuracy modestly without unit tests and more with execution.
numbers: Spider SQL: +2-3% from code explanation; +9% on the hardest queries. TransCoder and MBPP: up to +12% with unit tests plus explanation; explanation alone +2-3% on code translation.
quote: code execution plays an important role in SELF-DEBUGGING
limits: Codex, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, StarCoder. Gains partly rely on execution feedback.
agent_relevance: A human debugging strategy (rubber duck) transfers modestly. Real execution feedback does most of the work.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) LDB: Large Language Model Debugger via Verifying Runtime Execution Step by Step
finding: Mimicking a human breakpoint strategy (segment into basic blocks, inspect intermediate variables, verdict per block) lifts pass rates over baselines.
numbers: Up to 9.8% gain over baseline across HumanEval, MBPP and TransCoder (abstract).
limits: Gain is relative to their baselines, and the strategy is bundled with real runtime values.
agent_relevance: A strategy that supplies fresh true data works; one that only restructures the model's own thinking works less.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: A reflect-and-retry loop with episodic memory reached 91% pass@1 on HumanEval versus 80.1% for GPT-4. Depends on the model writing good tests.
numbers: HumanEval Python 91.0 vs GPT-4 80.1; Leetcode Hard Python 15.0 vs 7.5; MBPP Python 77.1 vs GPT-4 80.1 (Reflexion lower there).
limits: Authors warn flaky or wrong self-written tests give false positives or negatives. Huang et al. 2023 attribute such gains partly to oracle signals.
agent_relevance: Loop works only when feedback is grounded in real tests.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
finding: Failures of multi-agent LLM systems cluster in design, misalignment and weak verification, not in strategy choice. Weak task verification is a category of its own.
numbers: 1600+ annotated traces, 7 frameworks, 14 failure modes; kappa 0.88 on 150 traces. Shares: system design issues 41.8%, inter-agent misalignment 36.9%, task verification 21.3%.
limits: Multi-agent systems, not single-agent debugging.
agent_relevance: Invest in verification and role clarity before adding strategies.

source: Synthesis across opened sources (not a new study)
finding: Across 2023-2024 LLM debugging studies the pattern repeats: a strategy label (self-repair, scientific debugging, rubber duck, free agent) changes pass rates by single digits unless it brings new true information (human diagnosis, tests, runtime values, correct files).
numbers: Olausson human feedback 33.30 -> 52.60; SWE-bench oracle files 1.96% -> 4.8%; AutoSD 113 vs 110 on D4J v2.0.
limits: Synthesis from the lines above. No LLM study found that directly replicates the Ko and Uttl cluster analysis.
agent_relevance: Schema priority: relevant knowledge and real execution evidence first, strategy choice second.

source: Gap note on search limits
finding: No 2020-2026 LLM study located that clusters model debugging behaviour into strategies and links clusters to success as Ko and Uttl did. Web search quota and Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv search APIs were exhausted or rate-limited, so this may be a search failure.
numbers: 0 direct replications located. 13 papers read via direct PDF download.
limits: Absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.
agent_relevance: Next pass: SWE-agent trajectory taxonomies and developer-versus-agent debugging comparisons.
